name: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
statement: No ranked voting system can be fair on every reasonable count at once.
statementAccent: fair on every reasonable count at once
meaning: With three or more options, no method for turning individuals' ranked preferences into a single group ranking can satisfy a short list of basic fairness conditions simultaneously — unless it simply hands all power to one person. It is not a flaw in any particular voting method but a mathematical limit on the whole class of rank-based methods.
mechanism: The conditions are unrestricted domain, that the rule works for every possible set of preferences; Pareto efficiency, that if everyone prefers A to B society does too; independence of irrelevant alternatives, that society's ranking of A against B depends only on how voters rank A against B, not on some third option; and non-dictatorship. Arrow proved that for three or more alternatives the first three conditions together force a dictator, so all four cannot hold at once.

examples.text: Three voters ranking three options in a rotating pattern produce pairwise majorities that cycle — A beats B, B beats C, yet C beats A — so no consistent group ranking exists, the pathology Arrow generalised.

Independence of irrelevant alternatives formalises the intuition that a losing candidate should not change who wins between two front-runners; real ranked methods violate it, so a spoiler who cannot win can still flip the result.

If preferences are restricted to a single left-right dimension — breaking unrestricted domain — the conditions become compatible and majority rule yields the median voter's choice, showing where the impossibility comes from.

variants.name: The Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem
variants.text: The strategy-proofness analogue: every non-dictatorial ranked method with three or more outcomes is manipulable, so voters can sometimes gain by ranking insincerely.

variants.name: The Condorcet paradox
variants.text: The ancestor and special case: majority rule can cycle even with rational voters, the local pathology Arrow turned into a universal impossibility.

whyItMatters: It is the founding result of social choice theory and a permanent caution against the search for a perfect voting system: every ranked method must compromise some fairness principle. It reshaped how economists and political theorists think about aggregating preferences and won Arrow the Nobel Prize.

working.lead: Expect every ranked method to compromise
working.text: when choosing a voting rule, accept that it must violate at least one fairness condition, and decide which trade-off you can live with.
rated systems like approval and score voting escape Arrow's theorem by using preference strength, though they face their own impossibility in Gibbard's theorem.

working.lead: Restrict the domain where you can
working.text: where preferences are genuinely single-peaked, majority rule regains coherence and a median-voter winner exists.

limits: The theorem constrains only ordinal, ranked aggregation. Cardinal or rated methods — approval voting, score voting — fall outside it because they use preference-strength information that its framework excludes, though they do not escape impossibility entirely, being subject instead to the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem on manipulability. Independence of irrelevant alternatives is the most contested condition, some arguing it is too strong. And the result depends on unrestricted domain: realistic single-peaked preferences can restore a fair rule. The mathematics is settled; its practical significance is debated.
misreadings: It does not say democracy is impossible or that all voting is worthless — only that no ranked method is perfect on every count at once. And it applies to ranked systems specifically: rated methods sidestep it, so 'no fair voting system exists' overstates a theorem about ordinal aggregation.
origin: Proved by the economist Kenneth Arrow in his 1951 book Social Choice and Individual Values, derived from his doctoral thesis; he won the 1972 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, the youngest economics laureate.
